scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The genre originated in the second half of the 1950s, influenced by Colombian and Peruvian cumbia.
It gained national scope in the 1990s when it became popular among the lower classes in the main urban centers of the Río de la Plata basin.
Key early groups included Los Wawancó (formed 1955) and Los Cumbiambas (1964).

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Cumbia is used for social events and parties to provide a light, romantic, or humorous atmosphere.
Cumbia villera serves as a medium for social commentary, exploring themes of crime, drug abuse, and inequality, often incorporating elements of prison culture.
Today it is a living tradition.

narration: Clothing is a central characteristic; bands often wear matching, specialized costumes or exclusive clothes.
The primary setting is the 'bailanta,' a large dancing hall.
Digital cumbia is associated with modern clubs like Zizek Club in Buenos Aires.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Gilda (the 'saint' of cumbia), Pablo Lescano (creator of cumbia villera), Antonio Ríos, Los Palmeras, Ráfaga, and Los Wawancó.
Modern exponents include L-Gante in the cachengue/RKT style.

Variants include Cumbia Santafesina (Santa Fe, accordion or guitar-led), Cumbia Norteña (Northern Argentina, guitar and keyboard-driven), Cumbia Villera (urban shantytowns), and Digital Cumbia (electronic/urban).
Derived from Colombian cumbia; influenced by Argentine folk styles like chamamé, guaracha, and cuarteto, as well as flamenco and Peruvian cumbia.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Argentine cumbia is parent of Cumbia colombiana: The original rhythm that was imported and adapted in Argentina.
Argentine cumbia is influence of Chamamé: A local folk style that fused with cumbia, especially in the Litoral region.
Argentine cumbia is sibling of Cuarteto: Another major pillar of the Argentine 'movida tropical'.
